questions.q: What attack was mitigated with the LSA protection?
a: LSA Protection was introduced as part of the Pass-the-Hash mitigations. It helps protect the Local Security Authority process from unauthorized access and credential theft techniques associated with Pass-the-Hash attacks.

questions.q: What change mitigates brute-force authentication attacks?
a: The Allow Administrator account lockout policy was introduced to help mitigate brute-force authentication attacks. It allows the built-in Administrator account to be subject to account lockout controls after repeated failed authentication attempts.

questions.q: Compare the template with the actual local policies (Effective State).
a: In Policy Analyzer, compare the imported template with the machine's Effective State. The comparison should display the requested 8 items.

questions.q: Why are two of them grayed out in the effective policy?
a: The two entries are grayed out because Policy Analyzer does not have an applicable effective value for those particular settings on the local machine. In other words, the settings are not directly defined or resolved in the effective local policy, so Policy Analyzer displays them as unavailable rather than as active configured values.

questions.q: What is the recommended setting regarding the apps source?
a: Open: Settings → Apps → Apps & features
The recommended configuration is to restrict the installation source to trusted applications, preferably Microsoft Store only, where the option is available.
This reduces the risk of users installing potentially unsafe applications from unknown sources.

questions.q: Choose three Windows permissions that you would toggle on/off to improve privacy.
a: Three suitable categories are:
bullets: Location — Disable access for applications that do not require location information.
Camera — Disable camera access for applications that do not need to use the camera.
Microphone — Disable microphone access for applications that do not require audio input.
after: These settings reduce unnecessary access to personal information and hardware.

questions.q: Which option is actively protecting the system from malware being inadvertently installed? Check if it is enabled by default.
a: The relevant protection is Real-time protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus.

Real-time protection continuously monitors files, programs, and activities for malware and other threats. On a standard Windows installation, Real-time protection is normally enabled by default unless it has been disabled by the user, administrator, or another security product.

questions.q: Enable the option to control access to folders as protection against ransomware.
a: The required feature is: Controlled folder access
It is available under:
questions.code: Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Ransomware protection → Manage ransomware protection
after: Controlled folder access helps prevent untrusted applications from making unauthorized changes to protected folders. Enable the feature.

questions.q: Which option avoids malicious apps switching real-time protection off?
a: The required option is: Tamper Protection
Tamper Protection helps prevent unauthorized applications or malicious software from changing important Microsoft Defender Antivirus settings, including real-time protection.

questions.q: Enable PUP protection in App & browser control.
a: PUP means Potentially Unwanted Program.
Open: Windows Security → App & browser control → Reputation-based protection
Enable the option for potentially unwanted application protection.
This helps prevent users from downloading or installing applications that may be unwanted or potentially harmful even though they may not meet the definition of traditional malware.

questions.q: In Exploit protection, what is DEP used for? Give a specific example or use case.
a: Data Execution Prevention (DEP) helps prevent code from being executed from memory areas that are intended to contain data. For example, if a vulnerable application receives more data than a memory buffer can safely hold, an attacker may attempt to place executable code into that buffer and run it. DEP can help block execution from that data memory area, reducing the impact of this type of memory-based attack.

a: The Memory integrity option is located at:

after: The setting is called: Memory integrity

questions.q: Try to enable Memory integrity and explain what happens.
a: Attempt to turn Memory integrity on. The result depends on the configuration of the VM.
Windows may allow the feature to be enabled, request a restart, or report incompatible drivers that prevent the feature from being enabled.

Answer: After attempting to enable Memory integrity, Windows displayed: After attempting to enable Memory integrity, Windows displayed an incompatible drivers warning. The feature could not be enabled because one or more incompatible drivers were detected. Windows recommended reviewing the incompatible driver information before enabling Memory integrity. If Windows reports incompatible drivers, record the driver information shown in the warning. If Windows successfully enables the feature but requires a restart, mention that instead.

questions.q: Verify that NetBIOS over TCP is disabled for all interfaces using PowerShell.
a: Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
questions.code: Get-CimInstance Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration -Filter "IPEnabled = True" | Select-Object Description, TcpipNetbiosOptions
after: The TcpipNetbiosOptions value should be: 2
Value 2 indicates that NetBIOS over TCP/IP is disabled.
Check every IP-enabled network interface shown in the output.
Result: If all interfaces show 2, the machine complies with the policy. If any interface shows another value, that interface does not comply with the policy.
